summary:
RIMLIGHT is a browser-based mission planner. It shows whether a lander at a chosen place and date on the Moon will have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication.
At the lunar south pole, the Sun and Earth stay within a few degrees of the horizon. A ridge or crater rim a few kilometres away can decide whether a mission succeeds. Coordinates alone don't reveal this. Our tool computes it from NASA LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons ephemerides for 26 places. These include Artemis III candidate regions, historical landing sites and VIPER's planned CLPS target, and users can also enter any other coordinate.
For each scenario, it simulates panel output, battery charge and gaps in Earth view, and compares places or dates side by side using the same hardware. The results are stated as plain conditions rather than a hidden score. It can also search for better dates or nearby places, with a research goal as an optional filter.
Example: Shackleton Rim's catalogue point loses power and never sees Earth during the default seven-day mission. A ridge 1.9 km away gets continuous sunlight.
This turns landing-site selection into a transparent, testable decision for planners, students and the public.
details:
RIMLIGHT is a mission planner that runs in the browser. You pick places on a 3D globe of the Moon. A place can be one of 26 source-labelled points (south-polar research sites, Apollo and CLPS landing sites, Artemis III candidate regions, VIPER's planned Mons Mouton target), a point on a ±3 km map around a polar site, or any coordinate you type or click. Then you choose a start date, a mission length and the lander hardware.

For each scenario the app shows:

- where the Sun and Earth are against the real terrain horizon

- when terrain hides them

- how much power a solar panel produces

- when the battery falls below its reserve

- how long the lander goes without a line of sight to Earth

Scenarios are compared side by side with the same hardware. Each result card answers two questions in plain words: "Power?" and "See Earth?". A search panel can test every start date for a place, or every place for a date. It keeps only the options that meet the battery and Earth-view limits, and a research goal from NASA's criteria can be added as a filter.

Offline, Python scripts query JPL Horizons and ray-march terrain horizons in 3,600 directions out to 250 km. They use LOLA DEMs: 5 m/px near the site, 80 m/px regionally, and the global map elsewhere. The browser runs the visibility, power and battery model locally, so there is no server, every change updates instantly, and the app works offline.

Benefits

- It makes a hidden effect visible: at the south pole a few hundred metres of terrain decide power and communication.

- It is transparent: there is no hidden score. Every number links to its NASA source and its model limits.

- It is validated: the ephemerides were checked against independent JPL queries, the horizons for numerical convergence, and the sunlight results against NASA's published polar illumination maps. The project has more than 800 automated tests.

Intended impact

We want mission planners, students and the public to be able to test landing-site and timing decisions themselves, for example "the ridge 1.9 km away instead of the crater wall", "three days later" or "April instead of November", and see why one option works.

Tools

- Data processing: Python (NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, PyProj, Skyfield, Requests, Matplotlib)

- App: TypeScript, React, three.js / React Three Fiber, Web Workers, Vite

- Testing: Vitest, pytest, GitHub Actions

- Data: NASA LOLA DEMs (PGDA, PDS), JPL Horizons, NASA Moon Trek, LROC imagery, Blue Marble

- Hardware: standard laptops only; no special hardware

Creativity

The app shows the terrain horizon, the moving Sun and Earth, and the battery on one time cursor, in 3D and as charts, so cause and effect can be seen together. Any coordinate on the Moon can be checked, and the app suggests better dates or places instead of only reporting results.

Factors we considered

- Scientific honesty: no invented data, results labelled with their resolution, and model limits shown on screen.

- Sites are research points, not certified landing sites.

- Earth view means line of sight, not a guaranteed radio link.

- Accessibility (keyboard, mobile), offline use, and fast loading.
